entry.title: Reliable Message Queue Consumption for Long-Running EdTech Cleanup Jobs
entry.summary: Short answer: consume cleanup work with a bounded worker, make the operation idempotent, acknowledge only after durable success, and send repeatedly failing messages to a dead-letter queue. The least complex design is usually a long-running worker process, not a web request stretched until a timeout gives up. For an education platform, a useful message might say that tenant school-42 has 18,240 expired upload records to remove. The web application records that work and returns. A worker reads it later, processes a bounded batch, and leaves a precise trail of what happened. Recovery is the design target: when the worker disappears between deleting records and acknowledging the message, the next delivery must be safe. That is the whole contract. entry.summary: You build a Slack agent that pulls GitHub issues, creates Jira tickets, and sends Stripe invoices. Ten people use it. Each person signs in with their own account. The agent uses a single service credential. Who is allowed to see which issues? Who can create invoices? When the agent makes 50 API calls in one user request, whose permissions apply? entry.title: Wells Fargo statements: using the half-empty 'Ending daily balance' column as a free parser test
entry.summary: Wells Fargo statements print an ending daily balance only on the last transaction of each day, leaving the column blank on other rows. That half-empty column is a free test for a parser: group rows by date, add each day's amounts to a running total, and compare with the printed balance. A mismatch tells you which day lost or mangled a row, not just that the month is off. I'm on the ZeraBooks team, where we convert a lot of these. The usual advice is "check that the month ties to the ending balance," which is right but coarse: a month that's off by 425.00 could be off anywhere in 30 days. The daily balance narrows it to one day, and it's sitting in the statement already.
